projects.name: Healthcare Platform Redesign — Patient Portal & Pharmacy
projects.summary: End-to-end UI/UX overhaul of a multi-module patient-facing mobile health platform — used across the full care journey.
projects.detail: The refresh was grounded in over 200 survey responses sent to BRGs (Business Resource Groups), revealing core user goals (efficiency, prompt communication, reliable information, quick task completion) and pain points (complex interfaces, lack of personalisation, overwhelming information, accessibility gaps). I led design across five modules: Patient mobile app, Phressia Dashboard, Shopify Pharmacy, Chatbot (PineApp Connect), and the internal Employee App. The visual direction was 'Calm & Simple with Morphism' — frosted glass effects, semi-transparent layers, and 3D icons — validated against a competing 'Immersive Realistic 3D' direction through A/B testing and two rounds of moderated usability testing with real patients.
process: Research phase: 200+ patient surveys via BRGs, user interviews, competitive benchmarking (Amazon, Bank of America, Fidelity Investments login patterns)
Wireframe Design → Usability Tests → A/B Testing → Moderated Testing (two full rounds)
VISUAL DESIGN IDEATION: Visual Preference Testing between Morphism and Immersive 3D concepts
Final Concept Design: Calm & Simple with Morphism selected — 3D icons for cards, line icons for list views, less clutter, clear bottom navigation
Homepage Wireframes refined based on user feedback: cleaner top nav, half-image carousel (Nielsen Norman backed), 3D icons on feature cards, overlay for extra features

Login Flow: Redesigned under Okta limitations — applied progressive disclosure (Hick's Law), split screen update (Login / Create Account / Continue as Guest), biometric options, reduced cognitive load
Wellness Center repositioned higher on homepage — research showed patient education improves outcomes; community engagement promotes health equity
Bottom navigation renamed: 'Visits' → 'My Visits', 'Get Care' → 'Find Care' (more action-oriented)
design_decisions: Chose Morphism over Immersive 3D: A/B test and moderated testing showed patients felt calmer and less overwhelmed with frosted glass approach — critical for a healthcare context where anxiety is already high
Progressive disclosure in login: Applied Hick's Law — the time it takes to make a decision increases with choices. Reduced login screen to three clear paths with progressive reveal
Half-image carousel indicator: Nielsen Norman research backs half-visible images as stronger affordance for scrollable carousels than dot indicators
Notification redesign: Differentiated actionable vs informational updates. Added swipe gestures (LinkedIn model) for quick management
Information categorisation in My Account: Grouped by actions-to-be-taken rather than data type — directly addressing the 'overwhelming information' pain point from research
Records highlighted for immediate attention: Surface critical records first — addresses 'prompt communication' and 'inconsistent updates' pain points
outcomes: 18% increase in patient bookings after appointment flow redesign
Won 4 award categories: Responsive Web & Mobile Design, Mobile Website, Patient Portal, Mobile Application
40% faster design system component creation using Claude + Figma Make
Reduced appointment drop-off rates significantly
57% of customers unlikely to recommend a poorly designed app — this refresh directly addressed brand perception risk
Validated through 2 rounds of moderated usability testing and A/B testing with real patients
projects.what_id_do_differently: I'd bring in accessibility testing earlier — we discovered some contrast ratio issues in the Morphism concept only at the moderated testing stage, which required rework. Running a dedicated accessibility audit in parallel with visual preference testing would have saved two sprints.
projects.business_impact: 57% of customers are unlikely to recommend a business if its mobile/website is poorly designed. The refresh directly reduced this risk while driving measurable booking increases and enhanced brand perception.

projects.name: Government Conversational AI Design System (Middle East)
projects.role: Senior UX Designer | Design System Lead
projects.summary: Built the UX design and component library for a conversational AI platform serving 700+ government services across the region — starting with traffic fine payment as the pilot service.
projects.detail: This was a unified government services platform for a Middle Eastern government. The brief was to create an AI chat experience that offers personalised, intelligent conversations for citizens — starting with traffic fine payment as a proof of concept across 700+ available services. I worked alongside Özgür Mutlu Genc (UI/UX Design Manager) and Kishor Sathe (UX/UI Lead, client side) on a 4-month engagement. The work spanned component audit, competitive analysis, user flow design, wireframing, style guide creation, UI design, and high-fidelity prototype delivery.
process: Component Audit: Audited existing web pages, extracted recurring elements, categorised screenshots by component type and frequency. Compiled a prioritised list of essential components for the design system.

Competitor Analysis: Examined direct and indirect competitors for conversational AI patterns. Observed sharp, modern, welcoming styling — aimed to evoke similar trust and approachability for government context.
User Flow: Mapped full service flow for traffic fine payment — how users interact with current service, what is working, key pain points identified
Key pain points addressed: Breadcrumb navigation (users lost in multi-step flows), search bar improvements, chart/graph interaction, adaptive conversation flows, robust privacy controls

Change Log process: Structured change management with dated requests — e.g. removing restriction status items that cannot be verified at runtime, replacing mobile/address selectors with proper form fields
Design System: 11+ services covered, 76+ components built, adaptive conversation flows, easy-to-navigate interface, self-improving AI technology hooks
High-fidelity prototype delivered with full presentation
design_decisions: Adaptive conversation flows over rigid decision trees: Government services have high variability — a rigid chatbot fails edge cases. Designed for contextual branching that could be extended to all 700+ services
Progressive disclosure for fine details: Citizens have varying digital literacy. Started with summary information, allowed progressive reveal of detail — reduced cognitive overload
Privacy controls as first-class UI element: Government AI handling personal data. Made privacy settings visible and accessible — not buried in settings
Breadcrumb navigation: Users were getting lost in multi-step payment flows. Explicit breadcrumbs reduced abandonment at payment confirmation step
Accessibility-first colour system: Government platform must serve all citizens. Contrast ratios and touch target sizes were non-negotiable constraints
outcomes: 35% reduction in B2B manual support tickets
76+ reusable components built into the design system
11+ government services covered in the initial system
4-month delivery from component audit to high-fidelity prototype
Scalable component library adopted across all digital touchpoints
Cohesive design language across government AI services
projects.what_id_do_differently: I'd push harder for citizen co-design sessions earlier in the process. We had strong competitor analysis and internal stakeholder input, but government services often serve users with very different digital confidence levels — more diverse user testing in phase one would have sharpened the accessibility decisions.

projects.name: Global Tire Manufacturer — B2C & B2B Redesign (APAC)
projects.summary: Led the discovery and UX strategy phase for a global tire manufacturer's APAC digital transformation — B2C and B2B website redesign across multiple markets.
projects.detail: I served as Lead Experience Designer on the client's APAC team alongside Pratibha (Digital Transformation Lead), Sithi (Visual Designer), and Charan (UX Designer & Researcher). The project began with a structured discovery phase focused on understanding what the client knew, benchmarking the client's existing APAC geo sites, and learning from competitors including Bridgestone, Michelin, Continental, and indirect competitors like Apple's digital experience approach. Key transformation drivers from the client included: increasing average session duration for new users to 3 minutes, reducing bounce rate from 53.2% to below 35%, converting 3%+ of website visitors to eNews subscribers, and crafting an omnichannel experience from digital to physical store.
process: Week 1 — Unravel: Kick-off workshops with key stakeholders, understanding business goals, defining success metrics, reviewing current state artefacts
Weeks 2–3 — Weave the Golden Thread: User interviews, CUG sessions, secondary research, competitor study, persona mapping, as-is customer journey & gap analysis, design language review

Weeks 4–5 — Realise the Potential: To-be customer journey, feature set derivation, technology landscape definition, finalising visual design language, high-fidelity prototype for critical path, sprint plan definition
Benchmarked US and international client sites across: User-centric design, personalisation, tire selector tool, comparison features, educational content, customer reviews, analytics/monitoring

Competitor analysis: Bridgestone, Michelin, Continental, Hankook, Cooper (direct); Apple, Amazon (indirect) — evaluated ease of use, navigation, search, product information, mobile features, AI capabilities
Conducted 34 one-to-one interviews with national and international users across English-speaking markets

Personas developed: Harry (Fleet Owner, Charlotte NC, 38) focused on maximising fleet efficiency and ROI; Smith (Field Service Technician, 30) managing work orders via mobile; Nathalie (Customer Service Representative) dispatching technicians and managing work orders
Journey maps created: Mapped quote creation, field maintenance, work order generation, invoice generation, and payment completion stages with pain points and opportunities at each stage
design_decisions: Persona-based personalised content over generic product pages: Fleet owners (B2B) and individual consumers (B2C) have fundamentally different decision journeys — separated content architecture accordingly
Tire selector tool as primary homepage CTA: Research showed users arrive knowing their vehicle, not the tire specification. The selector reduces friction at the most critical conversion point
Omnichannel journey design: Digital-to-store handoff was a key business goal. Designed appointment booking and store locator as seamless continuations, not separate experiences
Educational content integration: B2B customers (fleet owners) need technical data; B2C customers need guidance. Content architecture served both without overwhelming either
Component library approach: Designing a governed system rather than bespoke pages — directly enabled the 32% reduction in front-end development time
outcomes: 32% reduction in front-end development time via governed design system
100% visual consistency across global APAC markets
Future-ready APAC design roadmap delivered
34 one-to-one user interviews conducted across national and international markets
Full double-diamond discovery delivered: stakeholder workshops, personas, as-is/to-be journey maps, information architecture, high-fidelity prototype
projects.what_id_do_differently: The fleet owner (B2B) persona was developed later in the process than ideal — we started with a B2C lens and had to substantially restructure the IA mid-discovery when B2B requirements became clearer. Starting with dual-track persona work in week one would have saved time and produced a sharper architecture sooner.

projects.name: Global Fashion Retailer — E-Commerce Design System
projects.summary: Built the Atomic Design system for a global fashion retailer's e-commerce platform — mobile and web — establishing 100% visual consistency across global markets.
projects.detail: Designed and documented a comprehensive Atomic Design system covering the full e-commerce experience: product listing pages, product detail pages (PDP), shopping bag, checkout, size charts, promotional banners, and user account flows. The system defined a complete typographic scale (fs-xs at 9.48/12 through fs-6xl at 27.37/40), a full size/colour selection component library, shopping bag interactions, offer code management, and progressive shipping threshold indicators. All components were built accessibility-compliant with correct contrast ratios and touch target sizes, and the handoff documentation made engineering integration seamless.
process: Atomic Design methodology: Atoms (typography scale, colour tokens, icons) → Molecules (size selectors, colour swatches, rating components) → Organisms (product cards, PDPs, shopping bag) → Templates → Pages
Typography system: Defined 9-step scale from fs-xs (9.48/12, 0.79rem) to fs-6xl (27.37/40) — consistent across mobile and web

Product Detail Page (PDP): Size chart integration, band/cup selector, colour swatch system with +16 overflow pattern, model sizing notes (e.g. 'Mia is 5'10" and wears large'), multiple model photography system
Shopping bag: Progressive shipping threshold bar ($0 → $100), offer code module, cross-sell recommendations, save for later functionality
Size system: Comprehensive band (30–38) + cup (AA–DDD/F) matrix for bras; XS–XXL for apparel; Short/Regular/Long length variants with height guidance
Review system: Verified purchase indicators, fit/comfort/quality ratings, body type and size-worn attribution for social proof
Promotional system: 'New Savings', 'New Sizes', clearance pricing components, carousel for multiple marketing sections
Accessibility audit: Contrast ratios, touch targets, screen reader annotations throughout
design_decisions: Half-visible images for carousels: Backed by Nielsen Norman Group — stronger affordance that content is scrollable than dot indicators. Applied throughout PLP and shopping bag recommendations
Progressive shipping threshold: Research shows real-time progress toward a goal (the $100 threshold bar) increases average order value. Placed it contextually across bag, checkout, and PDP

Multiple model photography with size attribution: Fashion UX research shows customers convert better when they can find a model with their measurements. Designed the model note system (height + size worn) as a first-class component
+16 overflow pattern for colour/size variants: Avoids overwhelming the PDP with excessive options while maintaining discoverability — clicking reveals full range

Atomic Design over page templates: The global scale of this retailer (multiple markets, seasonal campaigns, constant new launches) demands a system, not pages. Atoms compose into organisms that can be recombined for any campaign without breaking consistency
team: Siba Sankar Kabi (UX/UI Designer, Design System Lead)
Cross-functional team with client product and engineering
outcomes: 100% visual consistency across global markets
Full accessibility compliance across all components
Seamless engineering handoff with comprehensive Figma documentation
32% reduction in front-end development time (design system governance)
Atomic Design system covers full e-commerce journey from PLP through checkout
Typography scale, colour tokens, and component library delivered
projects.what_id_do_differently: I'd establish a single source of truth for size data earlier. The size chart component required multiple revisions because size data came from different systems (bras vs apparel vs lingerie each had different sizing logic). A data audit before design work started would have prevented late-stage rework.

ux_knowledge._source: Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com) — the world's leading UX research and consulting firm, founded by Jakob Nielsen and Don Norman.
ux_knowledge._note: Use this knowledge to answer UX methodology, theory, and process questions. Always connect concepts to real project experience where relevant.

usability.definition: Usability is a quality attribute that assesses how easy user interfaces are to use. It encompasses both the design characteristic itself and methods for improving ease-of-use during development.
five_components: Learnability — How quickly users accomplish basic tasks on first encounter
Efficiency — Speed of task performance once users understand the design
Memorability — Ease of regaining proficiency after periods of non-use
Errors — Frequency, severity, and recoverability from user mistakes
Satisfaction — Overall pleasantness and subjectivity of the experience
usability.why_it_matters: On the web, usability is a necessary condition for survival. Users abandon difficult websites immediately. Investing roughly 10% of project budget on usability typically doubles quality metrics.
usability.how_to_improve: The fundamental method is user testing with representative users performing realistic tasks. Test with ~5 users to identify major problems. Use iterative design, testing between refinements.

ten_heuristics.name: Visibility of System Status
ten_heuristics.principle: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.
ten_heuristics.why: Builds predictability and trust. Users need to understand prior interaction outcomes and know what comes next.
ten_heuristics.example: Progress bars, loading spinners, breadcrumbs, 'You Are Here' mall map indicators.

ten_heuristics.name: Match Between System and Real World
ten_heuristics.principle: The design should speak the users' language. Use words, phrases, and concepts familiar to the user, rather than internal jargon.
ten_heuristics.why: Reduces cognitive load. Design should follow real-world conventions and natural logical ordering.
ten_heuristics.example: Stovetop controls positioned to match heating element layouts. Shopping cart icon for e-commerce.

ten_heuristics.name: User Control and Freedom
ten_heuristics.principle: Users often perform actions by mistake. They need a clearly marked emergency exit to leave the unwanted action without going through an extended process.
ten_heuristics.why: Prevents frustration and builds confidence. Freedom to undo reduces the cost of errors.
ten_heuristics.example: Undo/Redo functions, Cancel buttons, browser Back button, Ctrl+Z.

ten_heuristics.name: Consistency and Standards
ten_heuristics.principle: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Follow platform and industry conventions.
ten_heuristics.why: Reduces cognitive load. Users' expectations are shaped by other products they use regularly (Jakob's Law).
ten_heuristics.example: Hotel check-in counters consistently at the entrance. Save icon universally represented as a floppy disk.

ten_heuristics.name: Error Prevention
ten_heuristics.principle: Good error messages are important, but the best designs carefully prevent problems from occurring in the first place. Prefer prevention over recovery.
ten_heuristics.why: Preventing errors is always cheaper than fixing them after the fact. Constraints and confirmation dialogs save user effort.
ten_heuristics.example: Guard rails on mountain roads. Form validation before submission. Confirmation dialogs for irreversible actions.

ten_heuristics.name: Recognition Rather Than Recall
ten_heuristics.principle: Minimize the user's memory load by making elements, actions, and options visible. The user should not have to remember information from one part of the interface to another.
ten_heuristics.why: Humans have limited short-term memory. Interfaces that promote recognition reduce required cognitive effort significantly.
ten_heuristics.example: Visible navigation menus vs. memorized commands. Recently used files list in apps.

ten_heuristics.name: Flexibility and Efficiency of Use
ten_heuristics.principle: Shortcuts — hidden from novice users — may speed up interaction for expert users so the design caters to both inexperienced and experienced users.
ten_heuristics.why: Accommodates different skill levels. Accelerators like keyboard shortcuts, personalization and customization improve expert productivity.
ten_heuristics.example: Keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V). Power user modes. Customisable dashboards.

ten_heuristics.name: Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
ten_heuristics.principle: Interfaces should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed. Every extra unit of information competes with relevant information and diminishes its visibility.
ten_heuristics.why: Visual noise reduces signal strength. Focused design supports primary user goals without distracting decorative elements.
ten_heuristics.example: Google's homepage. Apple product pages. Decluttered checkout flows.

ten_heuristics.name: Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors
ten_heuristics.principle: Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no error codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.
ten_heuristics.why: Error recovery is inevitable. Clear, actionable error messages reduce user frustration and support task completion.
ten_heuristics.example: 'Wrong Way' road signs. Gmail's 'Message not sent — Retry' with a clear action.

ten_heuristics.name: Help and Documentation
ten_heuristics.principle: It is best if the system does not need any additional explanation. However, it may be necessary to provide documentation to help users understand how to complete their tasks.
ten_heuristics.why: Some tasks are complex enough to require support. Documentation should be searchable, contextual, and action-oriented.
ten_heuristics.example: Airport information kiosks. Contextual tooltips. In-app tutorials triggered at the right moment.

design_thinking.definition: An ideology paired with a structured process emphasizing a hands-on, user-centric approach to problem solving that drives innovation and competitive advantage.
six_phases: Empathize — Conduct user research to understand what people do, say, think, and feel
Define — Identify user problems and unmet needs from research data
Ideate — Generate diverse, creative ideas addressing identified gaps
Prototype — Build tangible representations to test concept viability
Test — Validate solutions with real users and gather feedback
Implement — Execute the vision to reach end users (the most critical phase)
core_principles: User-centered — begins with real user data, never assumptions
Iterative — phases loop back, teams frequently return to research after prototyping
Flexible — functions as scaffolding, not rigid prescription
Scalable — applicable from small features to organizational restructuring
design_thinking.origin: The formal framework emerged in the 1990s through David Kelley, Tim Brown, and Roger Martin at IDEO, building on decades of human-centered design.

research_methods.overview: UX research has 20 primary methods organized across 3 dimensions and 4 product phases.

three_dimensions.attitudinal_vs_behavioral: Attitudinal captures stated beliefs (surveys, focus groups). Behavioral observes actual usage (usability testing, A/B testing, eyetracking). They often diverge — what people say differs from what they do.
three_dimensions.qualitative_vs_quantitative: Qualitative answers WHY and HOW — based on observing or hearing behaviors directly. Quantitative answers HOW MANY and HOW MUCH — gathered through measurement instruments.
three_dimensions.context_of_use: Ranges from natural/near-natural use to scripted use, limited product interaction, or no product interaction at all.

by_phase.strategize: Generative research — field studies, interviews, concept testing. Goal: find directions and opportunities.
by_phase.design: Formative research — usability testing, card sorting, tree testing. Goal: improve usability.
by_phase.launch_and_assess: Summative research — A/B testing, benchmarking, analytics. Goal: measure performance.

research_methods.top_recommendation: If you can do only one activity to improve an existing system, do qualitative (think-aloud) usability testing. It is the most effective usability improvement method.

journey_mapping.definition: A visualization of the process that a person goes through in order to accomplish a goal. It compiles user actions into a timeline, enriches it with thoughts and emotions, then condenses everything into a visual narrative.
five_components: Actor — the persona experiencing the journey; one user perspective per map
Scenario + Expectations — the situation addressed, including the user's goal and specific expectations
Journey Phases — high-level stages organizing the experience (e.g., discover, try, buy, use, support)
Actions, Mindsets, Emotions — user behaviors, thoughts/questions, and emotional responses throughout phases
Opportunities — insights revealing how to optimize the experience and address pain points

related_artifacts.experience_maps: Broader, generic human behavior without specific product focus
related_artifacts.service_blueprints: Internal business perspective supporting the customer journey — the operational 'how'
related_artifacts.user_story_maps: Tactical planning tool for feature implementation and sprint planning

journey_mapping.best_for: Scenarios involving multiple events, sequential processes, or multi-channel interactions requiring a comprehensive view.

service_blueprints.definition: A diagram that visualizes the relationships between different service components — people, props (physical or digital evidence), and processes.
five_components: Customer Actions — steps customers take to reach their goals
Frontstage Actions — visible employee or technology interactions with customers
Backstage Actions — behind-the-scenes support activities invisible to customers
Processes — internal steps enabling service delivery
Evidence — physical/digital props involved in service exchanges
organizing_lines: Line of Interaction — direct customer-organization exchanges
Line of Visibility — separates visible from hidden activities
Line of Internal Interaction — distinguishes customer-facing from support staff
service_blueprints.vs_journey_maps: Journey maps focus on the customer experience (the front stage). Service blueprints expose the organizational infrastructure behind it. Blueprints are 'part two' to journey maps.
service_blueprints.best_for: Complex, omnichannel scenarios involving multiple touchpoints and cross-departmental coordination. Excellent for exposing systemic weaknesses and root causes of service failures.

empathy_mapping.definition: A collaborative visualization tool that articulates what is known about a particular user type. Serves dual purposes: create shared understanding of user needs and aid in decision making.

four_quadrants.says: Direct quotes from user research — e.g., 'I want something reliable'
four_quadrants.thinks: User's internal thoughts and concerns, including unspoken worries — e.g., 'Am I dumb for not understanding this?'
four_quadrants.does: Physical actions and behaviors — e.g., refreshes page repeatedly, compares prices across tabs
four_quadrants.feels: Emotional state as adjectives with context — e.g., 'Impatient due to slow page loads'

empathy_mapping.types: Individual maps (based on single user) or aggregated maps (synthesizing multiple similar users — can precede persona development).
benefits: Removes bias and aligns teams on shared user understanding
Uncovers needs users may not consciously recognize
Creates digestible communication tool for stakeholders

usability_testing.definition: A researcher asks a participant to perform tasks, usually using specific user interfaces, while observing behavior and gathering feedback.

three_elements.facilitator: Guides participants through testing, administers tasks, asks follow-up questions without accidentally influencing behavior
three_elements.tasks: Realistic activities the participant might perform in real life — ranging from specific to open-ended
three_elements.participant: Should represent realistic users of the product

approaches.qualitative_vs_quantitative: Qualitative focuses on insights and problem discovery. Quantitative collects metrics like task success rates and time-on-task.
approaches.moderated_vs_unmoderated: Moderated involves direct facilitator interaction. Remote unmoderated uses platforms to deliver tasks independently.

usability_testing.think_aloud_method: Participants narrate their actions and thoughts during task performance, revealing behaviors, goals, and motivations.
usability_testing.sample_size: Five participants typically uncover the majority of usability issues in qualitative studies (Nielsen's Law of diminishing returns after 5 users).

personas.definition: A fictional, yet realistic, description of a typical or target user grounded in concrete research rather than assumptions.
core_components: Context for how they use the product
benefits: Foster empathy — make user groups feel tangible and real
Create shared vocabulary — personas serve as shorthand across teams
Combat design-for-everyone tendencies by focusing on specific individuals
Support recruiting testers, expert reviews, and analytics segmentation
personas.critical_principle: Do not add details that are irrelevant to the design. Every element should either influence decisions or enhance memorability.

card_sorting.definition: A research method in which study participants place individually labeled cards into groups according to criteria that make the most sense to them.
card_sorting.purpose: Reveals user mental models and informs information architecture design, making content more discoverable and easier to navigate.

types.open: No predefined categories — users create their own groupings. Best for understanding how users think.
types.closed: Researchers provide fixed categories for validation. Best for testing existing structure.
types.hybrid: Mix of predefined and user-created categories.

card_sorting.sample_size: Qualitative studies: minimum 15 participants. Quantitative studies: 30-50+ for statistical validity.
card_sorting.best_for: Restructuring content organization, categorizing product offerings, designing navigation that matches user mental models.

mental_models.definition: A mental model is what the user believes about the system at hand. These beliefs — whether accurate or not — guide how users predict system behavior.
mental_models.how_they_work: Mental models develop through users' existing knowledge and past experiences. Each user constructs their own unique model based on individual background, creating potential gaps between designer and user understanding.
design_application: Align interfaces with established user expectations (Jakob's Law — users spend most of their time on other sites)
Redesign systems to conform to user mental models when mismatches cause friction
Use think-aloud sessions to surface erroneous mental models early
mental_models.key_principle: Mental-model inertia is powerful. Established beliefs persist strongly. Succeed by respecting this resistance rather than fighting it.

design_systems.definition: A complete set of standards intended to manage design at scale using reusable components and patterns.

three_components.style_guide: Documentation covering branding (colors, typography, logos), content guidance (tone of voice), and visual/interaction design standards
three_components.component_library: Reusable UI elements with specifications: names, descriptions, customizable attributes, state variations, code snippets, implementation frameworks
three_components.pattern_library: Collections of grouped UI elements, layouts, templates, and content structures designed for reuse and adaptation

benefits: Enables rapid design replication at scale
Frees designers to focus on complex problems beyond basic UI tweaks
Establishes unified terminology across cross-functional teams
Ensures visual consistency across products and departments
design_systems.governance: Requires dedicated management: minimum one interaction designer, one visual designer, one developer. Ideally adds part-time researcher, architect, and content writer. An executive sponsor helps secure resources.
design_systems.implementation: Adopt existing systems (lowest cost) → Adapt existing to needs → Create custom proprietary system (highest investment). ROI justifies investment only when sustained, replicable design work is anticipated over years.
design_systems.when_to_invest: Design systems generate ROI when organizations anticipate sustained, replicable design work across years — not for one-off prototypes or proof-of-concept projects.

f_pattern_reading.definition: An eye-tracking research finding showing users read web content in an F-shaped pattern when content lacks formatting cues.
three_movements: Horizontal scan across the upper content area (top bar of the F)
Second shorter horizontal scan partway down the page (lower bar of the F)
Vertical scan along the left side of the content (stem of the F)

design_implications.problems: Users miss important right-side content. Critical information buried in paragraphs is skipped.
solutions: Front-load critical information in opening paragraphs
Use descriptive headings, subheadings, and bold text
Implement bullets, numbers, and visual grouping

f_pattern_reading.key_insight: Strong formatting and strategic content hierarchy override F-pattern scanning behavior.

heuristic_evaluation.definition: A usability inspection method where evaluators examine the interface and judge its compliance with recognised usability principles (the heuristics).
heuristic_evaluation.process: Each evaluator independently inspects the interface against the 10 Nielsen heuristics, identifying violations and rating severity. Results are then aggregated.
heuristic_evaluation.severity_scale: 0 = Not a usability problem, 1 = Cosmetic problem only, 2 = Minor usability problem, 3 = Major usability problem (important to fix), 4 = Usability catastrophe (imperative to fix before product is released)
heuristic_evaluation.evaluator_count: 3-5 evaluators find approximately 75% of usability issues. Fewer than 3 miss too many problems; more than 5 offers diminishing returns.
heuristic_evaluation.advantage: Quick, cheap, and requires no users. Best early in the design process to catch obvious issues before user testing.

jakob_law.statement: Users spend most of their time on OTHER websites. This means they expect your website to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.
jakob_law.implication: Designers can make users' lives easier by following established patterns and conventions. Users transfer expectations from prior experiences.
jakob_law.application: Innovate only where it adds clear value. Match existing mental models for navigation, form behavior, and interaction patterns. Reserve innovation for competitive differentiators — not standard UI patterns.
jakob_law.named_after: Jakob Nielsen, co-founder of the Nielsen Norman Group, who articulated this principle in 2000.

ux_concepts_glossary.information_architecture: The structural design of shared information environments — organizing, labeling, and creating navigation systems to help users find and manage information efficiently.
ux_concepts_glossary.interaction_design: Designing interactive products to support the way people communicate and interact. Concerned with the behavior of products — how they respond to user input.
ux_concepts_glossary.progressive_disclosure: An interaction design technique that sequences information and actions across several screens, presenting only the minimum necessary at each step to reduce cognitive load.
ux_concepts_glossary.affordance: A design property that signals how an object should be used. Visual affordances communicate possible interactions — e.g., a button looks pressable.
ux_concepts_glossary.gestalt_principles: Psychological principles describing how humans perceive visual elements as unified wholes — including proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, and figure-ground.
ux_concepts_glossary.hicks_law: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices. Reduce options to speed up decision-making.
ux_concepts_glossary.fitts_law: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target. Make important buttons large and close to likely cursor positions.
ux_concepts_glossary.cognitive_load: The total amount of mental effort being used in working memory. UX design should minimize extraneous cognitive load and support germane (learning-related) load.
ux_concepts_glossary.information_scent: The degree to which interface elements suggest the value and destination of content ahead, helping users decide whether to click a link or navigate in a direction.
ux_concepts_glossary.accessibility: Designing products usable by people with disabilities. WCAG guidelines organize accessibility around four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust (POUR).
ux_concepts_glossary.double_diamond: A design process model with two diamonds — Discover and Define (problem space) followed by Develop and Deliver (solution space). Popularized by the UK Design Council.
ux_concepts_glossary.mvp: Minimum Viable Product — the simplest version of a product that allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort.
ux_concepts_glossary.atomic_design: A methodology for creating design systems by breaking interfaces into atoms (basic HTML elements), molecules, organisms, templates, and pages. Created by Brad Frost.
ux_concepts_glossary.ux_maturity: The degree to which an organization has integrated user experience thinking into its processes, culture, and strategy. Ranges from absent to pervasive.
ux_concepts_glossary.kano_model: A model for prioritizing product features based on customer satisfaction. Categorizes features as Basic needs, Performance attributes, and Delighters (excitement factors).
ux_concepts_glossary.north_star_metric: A single metric that best captures the core value your product delivers to customers. Aligns the team around what truly matters for long-term product success.
ux_concepts_glossary.tree_testing: A technique for evaluating the findability of topics in a website's navigation. Tests the information architecture without visual design, using text-only hierarchy.
ux_concepts_glossary.contextual_inquiry: A field research method where researchers observe and interview users in their natural environment while they work, to understand how context influences behavior.
ux_concepts_glossary.diary_study: A longitudinal research method where participants self-report their experiences, behaviors, and perceptions over time in a structured journal or log.
ux_concepts_glossary.storyboarding: A sequence of illustrations or sketches depicting how a user would interact with a product or service in a specific context over time.
ux_concepts_glossary.value_proposition: A clear statement of the tangible results a customer gets from using your product. Answers: what it is, who it is for, and why it matters.
